name: Mini 4WD
blurb: Tamiya's 1:32 battery-powered kit racers, run on walled tracks with no remote control
title: Mini 4WD: Tamiya's Kit Racers, the Let's & Go Boom and Today
description: Mini 4WD are Tamiya's 1:32 four-wheel-drive kit cars, first sold in 1982. Booms in the late 1980s and 1990s made them a childhood staple in Japan and China.
answer: Mini 4WD (ミニ四駆) are small 1:32 scale model race cars from the Japanese company Tamiya: you build the kit, put in two AA batteries and let the car run along a walled track, with no remote control. They first went on sale in July 1982 and had two huge booms in Japan, in the late 1980s and in the mid-to-late 1990s, the second driven by the manga and anime Bakusō Kyōdai Let's & Go!!, which also spread the craze to China as 四驱兄弟. Tamiya still makes them, and cumulative sales passed 170 million by 2012.

body: A box held a plastic body, chassis, motor, gears and tyres that you snapped together yourself. Switch it on and it just runs straight ahead; on a track, side rollers ride along the walls to take the corners. Racing is about speed and staying on the track, which is where tuning comes in: faster motors, bearings, different tyres, extra rollers and weights. Cars tuned too far fly off at the corners, which every owner has seen.

body: Let's & Go!! follows the brothers Rettsu and Go Seiba and their cars Sonic Saber and Magnum Saber as they race up to a world championship. Dubbed into Chinese as 四驱兄弟 ("Four-Wheel-Drive Brothers"), it aired in mainland China roughly from the late 1990s into the early 2000s, and four-wheel-drive racers became a schoolyard craze.

Many Chinese children's cars were not Tamiya originals but cheaper look-alikes from domestic makers, most famously Auldey (奥迪) of Shantou, the company that later became Alpha Group (奥飞娱乐). Chinese media have reported that the company paid to bring related anime to Chinese TV to help sell its cars.

Yes. Tamiya never stopped making Mini 4WD; it still releases new cars and chassis, and since the Japan Cup's return in 2012 a third boom has been led largely by adults who raced as children. Old Chinese look-alike cars from the 1990s mostly turn up only second-hand.
